newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Nusamba says punish Busang culprits.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Nusamba says punish Busang culprits.

text.p: Indonesia's Nusamba Group, which is linked to President Suharto, said on Monday those involved in the Busang gold scandal should be punished but it did not plan legal action against the firm at the heart of the controversy.
"In my own opinion they should be punished," Nusamba chairman Muhammad 'Bob' Hasan said, referring to those involved in falsifying geological samples from the Busang discovery.
"They have made a lot of (problems). They should be punished," Hasan told a news conference.

But Nusamba would not take legal action against Canadian exploration company Bre-X Minerals Ltd, he said, adding that Nusamba had not incurred any financial losses from its involvement in the Busang project.
He said he believed the Indonesian government would investigate the scandal, adding that Nusamba had withdrawn from the Busang project in East Kalimantan province.

Nusamba had a 25 percent stake in Busang, its local partner PT Askatindo Karya Minerals has five percent, Bre-X has 45 percent, Freeport McMoRan Copper and Gold 15 percent and the Indonesian government the remaining 10 percent.
Freeport said on Monday it would notify Bre-X it was withdrawing from the Busang project.
Nusamba is 80 percent owned by three charities headed by President Suharto, and 10 percent each by Hasan and Suharto's eldest son Sigit Harjojudanto.

Bre-X Minerals Ltd released a report from Canadian mining consultant Strathcona Mineral Services Ltd in Canada on Sunday in which Strathcona said assays of test cores from the key area of Busang had shown no commercial gold content.
The Strathcona report also referred to falsification of assay values at Busang on an unprecedented scale.

Bre-X had earlier estimated gold reserves at Busang in Indonesia's East Kalimantan province at over 70 million ounces. But Bre-X stunned the mining world last month when it said the amount of gold might have been overestimated.
Hasan said he received a copy of the Strathcona report early on Monday, and that he would be informing President Suharto of Nusamba's decision to withdraw from the project.

He said the Strathcona report would make it difficult for junior exploration companies to raise funds in future, but added that Indonesia remained an attractive investment destination for the mining community because of its political stability.
Hasan said the scandal might prompt the Indonesian government to tighten mining regulations, with exploration companies being required to obtain independent second opinions on their discoveries.
"Ore samples should also be guarded well when being transferred from the field to laboratories...to make sure there is no tampering," he said.
"In business, sometimes you make money, sometimes you lose money," he said. "We did not lose money. Askatindo asked us to get involved in the project to help them get a good deal."
Nusamba took a 50-percent stake in Askatindo when mining giants such as Barrick Gold Corp and Placer Dome of Canada were involved in a bidding war for Busang.
Hasan said he was not angry or disappointed over the collapse of Busang. The publicity had made Indonesia known to many who did not know its location on a map.
